newsitem.title: JAPAN: Beijing visit will set tone for Albright on China.
newsitem.headline: Beijing visit will set tone for Albright on China.

text.p: With a successful tour of Europe behind her, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is setting her sights on China, were Monday's visit will set the tone for the second Clinton administration's handling of a critical and complicated relationship.

During last week's seven-day swing through Europe, Albright maintained a high profile, taking every opportunity to communicate her message to the world: NATO will expand but it is not a threat to Russia.

Now, as she prepares for the second major task of her nine- nation Europe-Asia trip -- establishing her relations with Chinese leaders -- Albright seems to be going out of her way not to make headlines.
Posing for photographs Sunday at the start of talks with Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, she declined to answer questions.
Her few comments on China in recent days essentially have restated U.S. policy, providing no specific insight on how she expects to approach the leaders in Beijing, including President Jiang Zemin.

The visit comes at a delicate time, with the death on Wednesday of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping. Her talks have been shortened to take place only on Monday and she plans to depart Beijing before Deng's funeral on Tuesday.

The stop takes on added importance because Albright overruled some China experts in deciding to go to Beijing now and because she is attempting to reclaim for the State Department from other U.S. agencies the lead on China policy.

Albright and other U.S. officials have signalled that they expect 1997 to be a year of extremely active U.S.-China diplomacy and they forsee relations with China, a rising superpower, as a key diplomatic challenge.
Undoubtedly, the memory of her predcessor's first trip to the Chinese capital in March 1994 looms as a shadow.

Then-Secretary of State Warren Christopher talked tough on human rights en route to Beijing, provoking Chinese anger that made the trip unpleasant and unproductive. It left Christopher so diplomatically bloodied he did not visit China again until last November, after it was known he would be retiring.
That trip, building on months of painstaking work, helped underscore both sides' desire, after a period of sharply-eroding ties, to establish a more stable relationship.

Christopher went out of his way not to make a big issue over human rights differences. He made clear such differences would not stand in the way of U.S.-China cooperation in other areas. He also negotiated a blueprint for increased high-level U.S.-China visits, including a summit expected later this year.
At one point, Christoper even praised Beijing for taking steps to improve civil rights.
Since then, the State Department's latest annual report on human rights worldwide found China's rights situation had worsened, with all dissidents now jailed or silenced.

Albright signalled during her Senate confirmation hearing last month that if there was no improvement on human rights, Washington would again sponsor this year a U.N. Human Rights Commission resolution criticising China's record.
She promised to "tell it like it is" to China on rights. But also stressed the Clinton line that Sino-American ties would not be held hostage to any one issue.

As her China visit drew closer, Albright has refused to say what if any decision has been made on the resolution, which in the past has greatly angered Beijing, or how she will balance rights against other issues, including arms proliferation.

"We are consulting with the co-sponsors at the European Union about going forward with such a resolution, the possibility of it, and it is something on our minds as we go forward with assessing where the Chinese situation is on human rights," she said in Seoul on Saturday.
